title: US Space Force Selects L3Harris to Provide Advanced Tracking Satellites for America’s Missile Defense
summary: L3Harris Technologies has received a contract from the U.S. Space Force’s Space Development Agency (SDA) to produce 18 Accelerated Missile Defense Tranche 3 (AMDT3) satellites to support the Golden Dome for America’s space-based capabilities.
body_text: MELBOURNE, Fla., July 13, 2026 — L3Harris Technologies (NYSE: LHX) has received a contract from the U.S. Space Force’s Space Development Agency (SDA) to produce 18 Accelerated Missile Defense Tranche 3 (AMDT3) satellites to support the Golden Dome for America’s space-based capabilities. “L3Harris’ continued work in Indiana will deliver the next generation of space-based tracking capabilities that we need to protect the homeland and stay ahead of our adversaries,” said Sen. Jim Banks, R-Ind. “This is exactly the kind of industrial investment that strengthens deterrence.” These L3Harris satellites will enhance national security by detecting and tracking advanced missile threats. “We are proud to provide next-generation technology that will accelerate the nation’s ability to defend against emerging threats from hypersonic and ballistic weapons,” said Christopher Kubasik, Chairman and CEO, L3Harris. “As the industry’s Trusted Disruptor, L3Harris invested ahead of need by expanding production facilities and is ready to deliver missile defense satellites to support this national priority.” L3Harris’ AMDT3 satellites are equipped with medium-field-of-view payloads designed to provide fire control quality data for missile defense. With a newly expanded space manufacturing facility in Indiana and a new satellite integration facility in Florida , L3Harris will immediately begin manufacturing for delivery and launch of these tactical payloads. The new contract builds on the successful on-orbit demonstration of an L3Harris Hypersonic and Ballistic Tracking Space Sensor (HBTSS) satellite and infrared sensor payload the company developed for the Missile Defense Agency (MDA). L3Harris has more than 70 missile tracking and defense satellites on order, including five on orbit , between MDA’s HBTSS program and SDA’s Tracking Layer across Tranche 0, 1, 2 and 3. About L3Harris Technologies L3Harris is the Trusted Disruptor in defense tech. With customers’ mission-critical needs always in mind, our employees deliver end-to-end technology solutions connecting the space, air, land, sea and cyber domains in the interest of national security. Visit L3Harris.com for more information. title: Visa Reason Code 12.2: Your Tactical Guide to Winning Chargebacks
summary: Master Visa Reason Code 12.2 disputes. Learn specific evidence, response tactics, and prevention strategies to protect your revenue.
body_text: In the complex world of payment processing, chargebacks are an unavoidable reality for merchants. Among the myriad of reason codes, Visa Reason Code 12.2," Processing Error," often emerges as a perplexing challenge. This specific code signifies a cardholder' s claim that an incorrect transaction occurred due to a technical or operational glitch during the payment processing cycle. Successfully disputing these claims demands more than generic chargeback knowledge; it requires a tactical approach tailored to identifying processing errors and submitting precise evidence. These disputes, while seemingly straightforward, can significantly impact your bottom line and consume valuable operational resources, especially if you' re unsure of the specific triggers or the most effective defense strategies. Merchants often struggle to identify the root cause and compile the necessary evidence for a successful dispute representment. This comprehensive guide will demystify Visa Reason Code 12.2, breaking down its nuances, outlining the most effective chargeback defense tactics, and providing actionable steps to not only win these disputes but also implement preventative measures to safeguard your revenue against future Processing Error chargebacks. Visa Reason Code 12.2 Quick Reference Attribute Details Code Number and Name 12.2 – Processing Error Card Network Visa Category Processing Error Definition The cardholder claims that a transaction was processed incorrectly due to a technical or operational error. Key Challenge Merchants must prove the transaction was processed correctly, that the error was not their fault, or that the cardholder accepted the error. Primary Evidence Types Authorization logs, transaction receipts, system error reports, proof of correct processing, communication records, merchant processing statements Response Time Limit Typically 30 days from chargeback notification When Visa Reason Code 12.2 Appears: Real-World Scenarios Visa Reason Code 12.2 indicates that a transaction was processed with an error, leading the cardholder to dispute the charge. These errors are typically technical or procedural, rather than related to fraud or service delivery. Understanding the common situations where this code arises is crucial for developing an effective chargeback defense strategy. Our experience shows that many merchants encounter this when specific data points are incorrectly transmitted or interpreted by their systems or the payment gateway. Identifying the exact nature of the processing error is the first step in building a strong representment case. The following table illustrates common real-world scenarios that trigger a Visa Reason Code 12.2 chargeback. Scenario What Happened Why Code Triggered Defense Strategy Key Incorrect Currency An international customer purchased an item, but the transaction was processed in the wrong currency (e. g., USD instead of CAD). The cardholder was charged an unexpected amount due to currency conversion issues, perceived as a processing error. Provide proof the correct currency was displayed/selected, or the cardholder agreed to the displayed currency during checkout. Duplicate Transaction A customer' s credit card was accidentally charged twice for the same purchase due to a system glitch or manual error. The cardholder was charged for a transaction they only intended to make once, indicating a processing duplication error. Show that one transaction was voided/refunded, or that both charges correspond to distinct, authorized purchases. Incorrect Transaction Amount A customer' s purchase of $50 was mistakenly processed as $500, or vice versa, due to a data entry error or system malfunction. The amount charged to the cardholder' s account differs significantly from the agreed-upon purchase price, a clear processing error. Submit proof of the correct agreed-upon amount, authorization logs, and any subsequent attempts to correct the error. Invalid Transaction Data A transaction failed to capture essential data (e. g., incorrect merchant category code, missing authorization details) but was still posted. The cardholder' s bank identifies a transaction with incomplete or incorrect data that should not have been completed or posted. Provide complete transaction data, authorization codes, and evidence of successful processing according to network rules. System Outage/Glitch During a brief system outage, a transaction was processed but without proper encryption or secure protocols, leading to a card network flag. The card network or issuer flags the transaction as potentially compromised or improperly handled due due to system instability. Submit system logs demonstrating the temporary nature of the outage, subsequent successful transactions, and adherence to security protocols. Recurring Billing Error A subscription service charged a customer after they had cancelled, or charged an incorrect recurring amount. The cardholder disputed a charge they believed should not have occurred or was for an incorrect amount based on their subscription terms. Provide proof of cancellation terms, active subscription status, or correct recurring billing amount as per agreement. After reviewing these scenarios, it becomes clear that meticulous record-keeping and a tailored approach are paramount. Each situation demands specific evidence to counteract the cardholder' s claim effectively. Without precise documentation of every transaction detail and communication, merchants face an uphill battle in disputing these processing error chargebacks. The Evidence You Must Provide for Visa Reason Code 12.2 Successfully defending against a Visa Reason Code 12.2 chargeback hinges entirely on providing precise, irrefutable evidence that demonstrates the transaction was processed correctly, or that the processing error, if it occurred, was rectified or accepted by the cardholder. General evidence will not suffice; you must compile documents and data points that directly address the specific nature of the alleged processing error. The acquiring bank and Visa require a clear, concise, and well-supported representment package. The more thoroughly you can illustrate the correct processing of the transaction or the resolution of any identified error, the higher your chances of winning the dispute. Pay close attention to the format requirements, as improperly submitted evidence can lead to an automatic loss. Required Documents (Mandatory) The following documents are typically mandatory when disputing a Visa Reason Code 12.2 chargeback. These are foundational to proving your case. Document Type Required/Optional Purpose Format Requirements Authorization Log Required Proves the transaction received proper authorization from the issuer. Digital screenshot or printout, clearly showing date, time, authorization code, amount, and card details. Transaction Receipt Required Confirms the transaction details, amount, date, and merchant information. Digital copy (PDF) or scanned physical receipt, legible and complete. Merchant Processing Statement Required Shows the transaction as it was submitted and settled by your processor. Relevant section of monthly statement, highlighting the disputed transaction. Proof of Correct Processing Required Demonstrates that the transaction was handled according to the agreed terms and system settings. System logs, database records, gateway reports showing parameters and outputs. Supporting Evidence (Strengthens Case) While not always mandatory, these supporting documents can significantly bolster your representment package by providing additional context and reinforcing your claims. Document Type Required/Optional Purpose Format Requirements Customer Communication Optional Shows attempts to resolve the issue directly with the cardholder or their acceptance of the error. Emails, chat logs, call transcripts, clearly dated and showing relevant content. System Error Reports Optional If an error occurred, provides details on its nature, resolution, and confirmation it was not the merchant' s fault. Technical logs, IT reports, screenshots of system status. Terms & Conditions Optional Demonstrates that the cardholder agreed to specific terms (e. g., currency conversion rates, recurring billing cycles). Link to or screenshot of terms applicable at the time of purchase. Evidence Format Requirements When compiling your evidence for Visa Reason Code 12.2, adherence to formatting guidelines is critical. All documents should be clear, legible, and directly relevant to the disputed transaction. Ensure that dates, times, transaction IDs, and amounts are easily identifiable on all submitted materials. Organize your evidence logically, typically in reverse chronological order, and include a cover letter that clearly references each piece of documentation. Most card networks prefer digital submissions in PDF format. Avoid sending excessively large files or images that are difficult to read, as this can delay processing or lead to your evidence being overlooked. Step-by-Step Response Strategy for Visa Reason Code 12.2 Responding to a Visa Reason Code 12.2 chargeback requires a methodical and timely approach. A well-executed representment strategy can turn a potential loss into a win, protecting your revenue and reducing the operational burden. The key is to act swiftly, gather precise evidence, and present your case clearly and concisely. This section outlines a tactical framework for addressing these processing error disputes. From the moment you receive the chargeback notification to the final submission of your evidence package, each step is crucial for increasing your chances of a successful outcome. Practitioners note that the most effective representment cases often highlight the specific point of agreement or correction that invalidates the cardholder' s claim. First 24 Hours: What to Do Immediately Swift action in the initial hours after receiving a Visa 12.2 chargeback notification is critical. Delays can compromise your ability to gather evidence and meet strict deadlines. Step Action Description 1 Acknowledge Notification Confirm receipt of the chargeback notice from your payment processor. Note the exact date and time. 2 Identify Transaction Locate the original transaction in your system using the provided transaction ID, date, and amount. 3 Review Chargeback Details Carefully read the reason code and any accompanying notes from the issuer. Understand the specific claim of processing error. 4 Freeze Funds (Optional) If you haven' t already, ensure the disputed amount is held or deducted from your account. 5 Assign Responsibility Designate a team member or department to lead the investigation and representment process. 6 Check for Duplicates Verify if any previous refunds or adjustments were made for this specific transaction. Building Your Evidence Package Once immediate actions are taken, the focus shifts to compiling a robust evidence package. This is where you gather the documents and data to directly counter the cardholder' s claim. Step Action Description 1 Retrieve Authorization Records Pull the original authorization log showing the issuer' s approval for the transaction. 2 Locate Transaction Receipts Find the customer' s receipt, whether digital or physical, confirming the purchase details. 3 Extract System Logs Access your payment gateway or internal system logs to show how the transaction was processed. Look for currency, amount, and data integrity. 4 Document Communication Gather all correspondence with the cardholder regarding the transaction, especially if an error was discussed or resolved. 5 Verify Terms & Conditions If applicable, retrieve the T&Cs the cardholder agreed to, particularly for recurring billing or international transactions. 6 Compile Merchant Statements Include relevant sections of your processing statements showing the transaction' s settlement. 7 Prepare a Timeline Create a chronological timeline of events related to the transaction and any customer interactions. Crafting Your Response Letter The representment letter is your opportunity to clearly articulate your defense, guiding the reviewer through your evidence. It should be concise, professional, and directly address the chargeback reason. Component Description Example Detail Introduction State the chargeback details and your intent to dispute. " Regarding Visa Reason Code 12.2 for transaction ID[XXXX], we dispute this chargeback as the transaction was processed correctly." Executive Summary Briefly summarize your key argument and the evidence that supports it. " Our records confirm authorization[Auth Code], and the transaction was processed for the correct amount/currency as agreed by the cardholder (see Exhibit A & B)." Detailed Explanation Provide a narrative explaining the transaction, addressing the alleged error point-by-point. " The cardholder' s claim of incorrect currency is refuted by our checkout process, which clearly displayed[Currency]at the time of purchase (Exhibit C)." Evidence Reference Clearly reference each piece of evidence by exhibit number throughout your explanation. " As shown in Exhibit D, our system logs confirm the single, authorized transaction was for $50.00, not $500.00 as claimed." Conclusion Reiterate your position and request the chargeback be reversed. " Based on the compelling evidence provided, we request the reversal of this Visa Reason Code 12.2 chargeback." Common Mistakes That Lose Visa Reason Code 12.2 Disputes Even with strong evidence, merchants can inadvertently lose Visa Reason Code 12.2 disputes due to common errors in their representment process. Understanding these pitfalls is crucial for avoiding them and maximizing your chances of success. Many assume that a" processing error" is always the merchant' s fault, but that's a misconception. Often, the error is an interpretation, or the cardholder agreed to the processing. The following table outlines frequent mistakes that undermine a merchant' s chargeback defense, along with their description and impact on the dispute outcome. By being aware of these, you can refine your strategy and avoid unnecessary losses. Mistake Description Impact on Dispute Late Response Failing to submit representment documents within the strict 30-day (or shorter) deadline. Automatic loss of dispute; no opportunity to present evidence, regardless of its strength. Generic Evidence Submitting general transaction records without specific data that directly refutes the 12.2 claim. Weakens the case; fails to address the specific" processing error" alleged by the cardholder. Lack of Specificity Not clearly explaining how the transaction was processed correctly or why the alleged error is unfounded. Leaves room for ambiguity; the reviewer may side with the cardholder due to insufficient clarity. Ignoring Communication Overlooking or not providing evidence of prior communication with the cardholder that resolved the issue. Misses a crucial opportunity to show the cardholder was aware, agreed, or that the error was rectified. Poor Formatting/Legibility Submitting unorganized, blurry, or difficult-to-read documents. Frustrates the reviewer, leading to quick rejection, as evidence cannot be easily verified. Assuming Fault Automatically accepting responsibility for the processing error without thorough investigation. Leads to unnecessary financial losses; many processing errors can be successfully disputed. Incomplete Documentation Missing key pieces of evidence like authorization logs, full transaction receipts, or relevant system data. Creates gaps in your defense, making it impossible to fully prove your case against the claim. Industry-Specific Tactics for Visa Reason Code 12.2 While the core principles of disputing Visa Reason Code 12.2 remain consistent, specific industries face unique challenges and opportunities for defense. Tailoring your strategy to your business model can significantly improve your success rates. The following tables outline tactical approaches for various industry sectors. E-Commerce Strategies E-commerce merchants frequently encounter 12.2 chargebacks due to the digital nature of transactions, including currency conversion issues and complex payment gateway integrations. Tactic Description Benefit Display Clear Pricing Explicitly show final price in cardholder' s local currency or clearly state currency conversion terms. Reduces" incorrect currency" claims by ensuring transparency at checkout. Detailed Digital Receipts Send immediate, comprehensive email receipts with all transaction details, including order ID, items, and total. Provides a clear record of agreed-upon terms, useful for all types of processing error disputes. Robust Gateway Logs Ensure your payment gateway captures and stores extensive transaction data, including authorization responses and processing parameters. Offers undeniable proof of how a transaction was processed, vital for countering claims of incorrect data. IP Address Verification Capture and store the customer' s IP address at the time of purchase. Helps confirm the geographical location of the cardholder, useful in currency disputes. Saa S & Subscription Defense Recurring billing models are particularly susceptible to 12.2 chargebacks related to incorrect billing cycles, amounts, or post-cancellation charges. Tactic Description Benefit Transparent Billing Cycles Clearly communicate billing dates, amounts, and renewal policies during sign-up and pre-renewal. Minimizes disputes over incorrect billing amounts or unexpected charges after cancellation. Cancellation Confirmation Send immediate email confirmation upon subscription cancellation, detailing the last billing date. Provides proof the customer was notified of their cancellation status, preventing post-cancellation chargebacks. Usage Logs Maintain detailed logs of customer account activity and service usage. Can demonstrate active service usage even if the customer claims an incorrect charge. Flexible Grace Periods Offer a brief grace period or prorated refunds for early cancellations to avoid disputes. Proactive customer service can prevent a chargeback from escalating. Travel & Hospitality Approach This sector often deals with complex booking systems, fluctuating prices, and international transactions, making it vulnerable to 12.2 claims. Tactic Description Benefit Booking Confirmation Details Send immediate, detailed booking confirmations outlining all charges, dates, and terms. Provides a clear record of the agreed-upon service and price, useful for" incorrect amount" or" duplicate" claims. Dynamic Pricing Transparency If prices fluctuate, ensure the exact price at the time of booking is clearly displayed and captured. Counters claims of incorrect pricing due to dynamic changes. Pre-Authorization Logs Maintain records of pre-authorization amounts and final settlement amounts, especially for incidentals. Clarifies charges for additional services or holds, reducing" incorrect amount" disputes. Multi-Currency Options Offer clear, selectable currency options at checkout for international guests. Reduces disputes related to unexpected currency conversions. High-Risk Merchant Tactics High-risk merchants, often dealing with higher transaction volumes or complex product categories, must be extra diligent in preventing and defending against 12.2 chargebacks. Tactic Description Benefit Enhanced Gateway Monitoring Implement advanced monitoring for transaction anomalies, especially for duplicate submissions or unusual amounts. Proactive detection of processing errors before they become chargebacks. Frequent System Audits Conduct regular audits of your payment gateway and internal processing systems for glitches or data integrity issues. Identifies and rectifies potential sources of processing errors. Detailed Internal Procedures Establish strict, documented procedures for manual transaction entry, refunds, and adjustments. Reduces human error that can lead to 12.2 chargebacks. Chargeback Management Solutions Invest in automated chargeback management tools to streamline evidence gathering and representment. Increases efficiency and accuracy in fighting disputes, improving win rates. Preventing Visa Reason Code 12.2 Chargebacks The most effective strategy against Visa Reason Code 12.2 chargebacks is proactive prevention. By implementing robust processes, leveraging technology, and maintaining clear communication, merchants can significantly reduce their exposure to these processing error disputes. While some errors are unavoidable, a comprehensive prevention strategy minimizes the potential for such claims. Focusing on prevention not only safeguards your revenue but also enhances operational efficiency and improves customer satisfaction. It requires a commitment to continuous improvement in your payment processing ecosystem. Our chargeback experts emphasize the importance of regular system checks and clear customer communication to preemptively address potential issues that could escalate into a Visa 12.2 chargeback. Process Improvements Refining your internal processes can dramatically reduce the likelihood of processing errors Improvement Action Impact Standardized Transaction Entry Implement strict, documented procedures for all manual transaction entries, adjustments, and refunds. Minimizes human error, such as incorrect amounts or duplicate entries. Double-Check Currency For international transactions, ensure the correct currency is selected and clearly displayed to the customer. Prevents" incorrect currency" disputes, especially in e-commerce and travel. Clear Cancellation Policy Ensure your cancellation and refund policies are unambiguous and easily accessible to customers. Reduces chargebacks related to incorrect recurring billing or post-cancellation charges. Regular Reconciliation Perform daily or weekly reconciliation of transactions between your POS/e-commerce system and payment gateway. Quickly identifies discrepancies or duplicate transactions before they become chargebacks. Staff Training Provide ongoing training to staff on proper payment processing procedures, error identification, and customer service. Equips employees to handle transactions correctly and resolve minor issues proactively. Technology Solutions Leveraging the right technology can automate error detection and prevention, adding layers of security and accuracy to your payment processing. Solution Description Benefit Advanced Payment Gateway Utilize a modern payment gateway with robust error handling, validation rules, and detailed logging capabilities. Automatically flags invalid transaction data or potential duplicates, preventing them from being processed. Fraud Prevention Tools Implement tools that monitor for suspicious transaction patterns, which can sometimes indicate processing anomalies. While primarily for fraud, some tools can detect unusual transaction volumes or values that might point to errors. Chargeback Management Software Employ dedicated software to automate the collection of evidence and manage dispute representment. Streamlines the defense process, ensuring timely and accurate responses when chargebacks do occur. API Integration Monitoring Use monitoring tools to ensure seamless and error-free communication between your systems and the payment gateway APIs. Detects integration issues that could lead to data corruption or processing errors. Automated Reconciliation Tools Implement software that automatic ally compares your sales data with your payment processor' s records. Provides real-time alerts for discrepancies, allowing for immediate correction. Customer Communication Proactive and transparent communication with your customers is a powerful tool for preventing disputes, including those related to processing errors. Strategy Action Outcome Detailed Receipts Send immediate, comprehensive digital receipts for every transaction, confirming all details. Customers have a clear record, reducing confusion and disputes over amounts or items. Proactive Notifications Send alerts for upcoming recurring charges, subscription renewals, or significant transaction events. Gives customers time to review and question charges before they hit their statement. Easy Contact Channels Provide clear and accessible customer service channels (phone, email, chat). Encourages customers to contact you directly to resolve issues, rather than initiating a chargeback. Transparent Policies Make your refund, cancellation, and billing policies easily findable and understandable on your website. Sets clear expectations and reduces disputes based on misunderstandings. Confirmation of Changes Send email confirmations for any changes to a customer' s account, order, or billing. Ensures customers are aware of modifications, preventing disputes for unexpected charges or altered terms. Visa Reason Code 12.2 Response Timeline & Deadlines Adhering to strict timelines is paramount when responding to any chargeback, and Visa Reason Code 12.2 is no exception. Visa establishes specific deadlines for merchants to submit their representment, and missing these windows almost guarantees a lost dispute, regardless of the strength of your evidence. The typical timeframe for responding to a Visa chargeback is 30 calendar days from the chargeback notification date. This 30-day window is critical for gathering all necessary evidence, crafting your response letter, and submitting your package to your acquiring bank. Your acquirer then reviews your submission and forwards it to Visa. It' s important to note that this is a general guideline, and specific situations or regional rules might alter this timeframe slightly. Always confirm the exact deadline with your payment processor immediately upon receiving a chargeback notification. Beyond the initial representment, the chargeback lifecycle can involve further stages such as pre-arbitration or arbitration. If the issuer rejects your representment, they may initiate a pre-arbitration (or" second chargeback" ), which typically comes with its own, often shorter, response deadline. Failing to respond to any stage of the chargeback process within the specified timeframe will result in the dispute being permanently lost, with the funds returned to the cardholder and potentially additional fees levied against your merchant account. Timely and meticulous adherence to these deadlines is therefore not just good practice, but a critical requirement for successful chargeback defense. Conclusion Navigating the complexities of Visa Reason Code 12.2, the" Processing Error" chargeback, can be a daunting task for any merchant. However, by understanding its nuances, meticulously preparing your evidence, and adopting a proactive prevention strategy, you can significantly improve your chances of success. This guide has provided a tactical roadmap, from identifying real-world scenarios to executing a step-by-step representment process and implementing robust preventative measures.

body_text: View all news Rockwell Medical Advances Quality and Regulatory Leadership 07/22/2026 Download (opens in new window) PDF 192 KB Names Brian Cox Vice President, Quality and Regulatory Compliance WIXOM, Mich.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Rockwell Medical, Inc. (the "Company") (Nasdaq: RMTI), a healthcare company that develops, manufactures, commercializes, and distributes a portfolio of hemodialysis products to dialysis providers worldwide, today announced that Brian Cox has joined the Company as Vice President, Quality and Regulatory Compliance. Brian Cox - Vice President, Quality and Regulatory Compliance at Rockwell Medical, Inc. Mr. Cox brings more than 20 years' healthcare experience spanning medical device development and manufacturing, quality, regulatory compliance, operations, and program management. His background includes senior roles at large global healthcare companies, including Abbott and Johnson & Johnson, as well as smaller, growth-oriented medical device manufacturers, giving him a broad perspective on how to build and scale quality systems in complex regulated environments. “We continue to evaluate opportunities that expand our capabilities, broaden our product portfolio, and serve additional areas of the renal care market," said Mark Strobeck, Ph.D. , President and CEO at Rockwell Medical. "As we advance these priorities, it is critical that we continue to invest in compliance, quality systems, and the regulatory capabilities required to support our long-term vision. Brian's extensive experience building and leading world-class quality and regulatory organizations will help ensure Rockwell continues to uphold the highest standards of product quality, safety, and compliance as we execute on our growth strategy." Throughout his career, Mr. Cox has led cross-functional teams responsible for quality systems, regulatory readiness, audit oversight, product development, program management, and design controls. Additionally, he has domain expertise in Class I, II, and III medical devices, regulated manufacturing environments, product launch readiness, and governance frameworks that support innovation, organization scalability, regulatory compliance, and long-term growth. “Rockwell Medical has built a reputation for quality, reliability and high-touch customer service that serves as a strong foundation for future growth and innovation," said Mr. Cox. “I am excited to join the Company at a pivotal point in the Company's history as it continues to strengthen its leadership position within the dialysis marketplace. I look forward to building on Rockwell's unrelenting commitment to quality and regulatory excellence, while ensuring our systems and processes support innovation, scalability, and the long-term needs of customers and patients.” Mr. Cox holds a Master of Information Systems from George Washington University, a Master of Business Administration from the University of Texas at Arlington, and a Bachelor of Science from St. Louis University. He is also a certified Project Management Professional (PMP) through the Project Management Institute. About Rockwell Medical Rockwell Medical, Inc. (Nasdaq: RMTI) is a healthcare company that develops, manufactures, commercializes, and distributes a portfolio of hemodialysis products for dialysis providers worldwide. title: How Consumer Spending Trends Are Shaping Self-Service Retail in 2026
summary: Consumer spending is changing. See the self-service retail trends shaping vending, micro markets, Smart Stores, and operator growth in 2026.
body_text: Consumers haven’t stopped spending. They’ve become more thoughtful about where, when, and how they spend their money. That’s one of the biggest takeaways from the 2026 Micropayment Trends Report from Cantaloupe and 365 Retail Markets. The report looks at transaction data from more than 621,000 connected devices across the United States and Canada between January and December 2025 (roughly $4.6 billion in self-service spend), alongside consumer spending insights from Mastercard SpendingPulse®. Overall consumer spending held steady in 2025, but shoppers became more selective. They looked for value, convenience, and speed in their everyday purchases. Self-service retail kept growing at the same time — just not evenly across formats or locations. For self-service operators, that combination creates a clear opportunity. The businesses that make buying easier, and use technology to run smarter operations, will be better positioned to grow. Cashless Payments Now Drive 78% of Vending Sales Today’s consumers expect shopping to fit into their busy lives. Whether they’re grabbing a snack at work, picking up lunch on campus, or buying essentials in an apartment building, they want the experience to be quick and hassle-free. Our data reflects that shift. In 2025, cashless payments accounted for 78% of all vending sales , up from 73% the year before. Contactless payments , tapping a card or using a mobile wallet, made up 85% of cashless vending sales , up from 78% in 2024. Micro markets remained nearly 100% cashless, and Smart Stores operate completely cashless. Mobile wallets continued to grow, reaching nearly 38% of cashless sales by year-end. That pace was more incremental than 2024’s surge, which suggests the behavior is settling in: physical cards still do most of the tapping at food and beverage vending. Either way, the consumer expectation is the same — quick, simple, contactless. Payment type also shows up in the basket. At vending machines, the average cashless ticket was $2.45 versus $1.57 in cash — a 59% difference. Meeting those expectations starts with the right payment technology . Cantaloupe’s cashless payment devices let operators offer the fast, secure checkout consumers already use everywhere else, whether a customer taps a credit card, or pays with a mobile wallet. Removing friction at checkout improves the customer experience — and, as the ticket data shows, it tends to lift spend. How Fast is Self-Service Retail Growing in 2026? The self-service industry is still growing, but not every location performs the same, and the growth curve is flattening in the more established formats. Food and beverage vending sales rose 5% year over year to $3.3 billion . Micro markets crossed the billion-dollar mark for the second straight year, reaching $1.13 billion in sales, up 13% , across 7,451 locations . Location growth for micro markets was 19.7% — healthy, but a step down from 28% in 2024 and 36% in 2023. That deceleration isn’t a warning sign. It reflects a maturing format and operators becoming more selective about where they expand. Instead of simply adding locations, they’re concentrating on the ones with the most opportunity. Making those decisions requires more than instinct. Connected software gives operators visibility into which products sell best, which locations perform strongest, and where inventory needs attention — so they can act on real-time data instead of reacting after the fact. With Cantaloupe’s Seed management platform , operators can monitor sales, inventory, machine health, and route performance from a single system. That means less guesswork, fewer unnecessary service visits, and more time spent growing the business. Average Ticket Size: Vending vs. Micro Markets vs. Smart Stores As buying habits change, consumers are also looking for more than traditional vending can always provide. Micro markets and Smart Stores create a more open, retail-like experience. They offer fresh meals, beverages, snacks, and everyday essentials, which gives shoppers more reason to build a larger basket. The report shows that difference clearly. The average vending transaction was $2.01 in 2025. Micro markets averaged $3.02 , and Smart Stores reached $4.49 — the highest average ticket of any self-service format. Smart Stores were also the fastest-growing format by a wide margin, expanding from 71 locations to 572 — a 705% increase in a single year . Total Smart Store sales are still modest at $6.3 million, so this is early-stage scale rather than a mature revenue line. But the adoption rate points to real operator interest and growing consumer acceptance. Why Routine Spending is the Most Reliable Growth Source One of the report’s strongest messages comes from the consumer side of the data. According to our Consumer Context data, routine, everyday spending is the most reliable source of demand. Grocery spending grew 2.3% year over year in 2025, driven largely by routine purchases tied to work, school, and home life — patterns that hold steady through the year and depend less on travel or seasonal swings. Consumers also traded down rather than opting out. Quick service restaurants grew roughly 5% year over year , outperforming other dining segments as shoppers looked for more affordable options. Restaurants, grocery, and fuel and convenience together account for about 60% of total consumer spend — a stable foundation for any self-service play that intersects them. Vending and micro markets benefit from that same demand: convenience at a lower price point. Knowing which locations capture it best — and why — is becoming a competitive advantage. Connected devices, cloud software, and real-time analytics let operators spot trends early. They can adjust product mix, refine pricing, reduce stockouts, and improve service schedules using actual performance data instead of assumptions. Self-Service Predictions for 2026 Cantaloupe’s outlook for the year ahead is steady at the base and faster at the edge: vending sales growing about 5%, micro market sales volume up 10.9%, amusement and gaming sales up 19.5%, and Smart Store cashless transactions climbing 167%. Amusement and gaming is worth watching for a different reason. The segment reached $178 million in total spend, up 16.9% , and while cashless made up only about 37% of transactions, it drove 79% of revenue . Players who pay cashless spend $6.01 per session versus $0.94 in cash, because card and mobile payments don’t interrupt play. What Self-Service Operators Should Do Next Consumer spending habits will keep evolving. New retail formats will emerge (like the Hot Hold and Shaffle units Cantaloupe highlighted at NAMA 2026). Expectations for speed, convenience, and flexibility will only increase. The operators that succeed won’t simply respond to those changes. They’ll use technology to stay ahead of them. Whether it’s modern payment devices , cloud-based management software, micro markets, or Smart Stores, Cantaloupe gives operators the tools to adapt as consumer expectations change. As the 2026 Micropayment Trends Report shows, consumers are still spending. They’re simply choosing the businesses that make shopping easier, faster, and more convenient. Operators who pair strong locations with connected technology will be best positioned to capture that demand — not just in 2026, but for years to come. Fast Facts Cashless payments now account for 78% of all vending sales , with contactless payments leading the way. Smart Stores posted the highest average ticket at $4.49 , outperforming vending and micro markets. Micro market sales grew 13% in 2025 , even as operators became more selective about new locations. Operators using connected payments and management software are better equipped to meet changing consumer expectations and grow their business. Article 5 Numbers From the 2026 Micropayment Trends Report Every Vending Operator Should Know We’ve pulled five of the most operator-relevant numbers to give you a taste of what’s inside. But the full report is where the real value is — the context, the trend graphs, and the consumer behavior data that explains not just what happened in 2025, but why, and what it signals for the year ahead. Amusement , Payments , Smart Stores , Vending 7 minute read Article Ready to Grow? Why Vending Operators Are Getting into Amusements Amusement machines are quickly becoming one of the fastest-growing opportunities in self-service retail. Here, we break down the trends, payment data, and technology making it easier than ever for vending operators to add games—and unlock new revenue streams. Business Management​ , Card Readers 5 minute read Article Why Vending Machines Need Contactless Payments If your vending machines still rely on cash, you’re leaving money on the table. Today’s consumers expect speed, ease, and the ability to pay with a tap. Find out how this small shift in payment preference is driving big results for operators — and why going contactless might be the smartest move you make this year. title: Nauticus Robotics Pursues Next Generation Ocean Sensing Infrastructure with Aquanaut® Platform
summary: HOUSTON, July 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nauticus Robotics, Inc. (NASDAQ: KITT, "Nauticus" or the "Company"), a leading innovator in autonomous…...
body_text: HOUSTON , July 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Nauticus Robotics, Inc. (NASDAQ: KITT, "Nauticus" or the "Company"), a leading innovator in autonomous subsea robotics and software solutions, today announced that it is actively pursuing opportunities to support next-generation autonomous ocean sensing infrastructure through its flagship Aquanaut® platform. As governments, research institutions, and commercial organizations seek improved methods for monitoring the world's oceans and critical subsea infrastructure, Nauticus believes autonomous robotic systems can significantly reduce the cost and complexity of deploying, inspecting, maintaining, and monitoring persistent subsea sensing networks. These networks have the potential to provide continuous streams of environmental and geophysical data while enabling greater visibility into changing ocean conditions and critical subsea assets. The world's oceans remain significantly under-sensored despite their increasing importance to environmental stewardship, offshore energy, subsea communications, scientific research, national security, and critical infrastructure protection. Nauticus believes this presents an emerging opportunity for autonomous subsea robotics to support the deployment and long-term operation of continuous ocean sensing infrastructure, creating a new class of persistent underwater monitoring capabilities. Recent advances in distributed fiber optic sensing, autonomous robotics, artificial intelligence, and subsea communications are enabling continuous ocean monitoring at a scale and cost that was previously impractical. The Company is currently participating in multiple collaborative proposal efforts with government agencies, commercial organizations, and academic institutions to evaluate future autonomous subsea sensing solutions. These opportunities include government- and commercially-sponsored feasibility studies focused on the deployment, monitoring, and long-term operation of continuous ocean sensing infrastructure. The proposal efforts span multiple geographic regions and are intended to support persistent monitoring of critical subsea infrastructure, environmental conditions, and other emerging ocean intelligence applications. Nauticus believes the Aquanaut platform is uniquely positioned to support these emerging applications through its ability to autonomously perform complex subsea operations while minimizing reliance on traditional surface vessel-intensive activities. The Company is collaborating with prospective industry participants possessing expertise in fiber optic technologies, deployment systems, offshore operations, geophysical analysis, and data acquisition to evaluate integrated solutions capable of enabling persistent subsea monitoring. By bringing together specialists across multiple disciplines, Nauticus believes autonomous robotics can serve as a foundational component of a scalable ocean sensing ecosystem that delivers continuous, high-quality subsea data while reducing operational costs and vessel dependence. "We believe autonomous robotics will play a transformative role in the next generation of ocean intelligence," said John Gibson, President and CEO of Nauticus. "The world's oceans remain one of our least continuously observed environments, yet they are becoming increasingly important to global infrastructure, environmental monitoring, scientific research, resource management, and national security. We are encouraged by the collaborative discussions currently underway and believe Aquanaut is uniquely positioned to help enable a new generation of persistent, cost-effective ocean sensing solutions. The breadth of engagement we are seeing from government, commercial, and academic organizations reinforces our confidence that autonomous subsea operations will become an increasingly important part of future ocean infrastructure. We believe this represents the beginning of a significant long-term market opportunity for autonomous subsea robotics, and we intend for Nauticus to be at the forefront of enabling persistent ocean sensing infrastructure around the world." While these activities are currently in the proposal and evaluation stage, and there can be no assurance they will result in awarded projects or commercial agreements, Nauticus believes its differentiated autonomous technology, growing industry engagement, and expanding ecosystem of collaborators position the Company to participate in this emerging market as it develops. About Nauticus Robotics Nauticus Robotics, Inc. develops autonomous robots for the ocean industries. Autonomy requires the extensive use of sensors, artificial intelligence, and effective algorithms for perception and decision allowing the robot to adapt to changing environments. The company's business model includes using robotic systems for service, selling vehicles and components, and licensing of related software to both the commercial and defense business sectors. Nauticus has designed and is currently testing and certifying a new generation of vehicles to reduce operational cost and gather data to maintain and operate a wide variety of subsea infrastructure. Besides a standalone service offering and forward-facing products, Nauticus' approach to ocean robotics has also resulted in the development of a range of technology products for retrofit/upgrading traditional ROV operations and other third-party vehicle platforms. Nauticus' services provide customers with the necessary data collection, analytics, and subsea manipulation capabilities to support and maintain assets while reducing their operational footprint, operating cost, and greenhouse gas emissions, to improve offshore health, safety, and environmental exposure. https://nauticusrobotics.com/ Cautionary Language Regarding Forward-Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of Section 21E of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the "Act"), and are intended to enjoy the protection of the safe harbor for forward-looking statements provided by the Act as well as protections afforded by other federal securities laws. title: How to Add an AI Scribe to MEDHOST EHR in 2026
summary: MEDHOST has no native scribe. Compare lightweight overlays and workforce platforms—and see which goes past the note to submit claims across your ED and floors.
body_text: You run a community hospital on MEDHOST, the EHR and EDIS vendor that has served community healthcare for more than 40 years, and you want visit and encounter notes written without pulling clinicians away from patients. The problem is that documentation eats the day. Physicians spend close to two hours on the EHR and deskwork for every hour of direct patient care [1], and family doctors log about 86 minutes of nightly "pajama time" finishing charts [2]. In the emergency department, the pressure is even higher. Here is the catch worth knowing up front: MEDHOST does not have its own AI scribe, so adding one means a third-party tool, and the options range from lightweight overlays to enterprise contracts to a connected AI workforce. This guide covers how a scribe connects to MEDHOST, a step by step rollout, and the tools worth shortlisting. Key Takeaway MEDHOST does not have a native AI scribe, so to add one you connect a third-party HIPAA-compliant ambient documentation tool. Lightweight cross-EHR scribes document and stop at the note, and enterprise ambient platforms document at scale but deploy like enterprise projects. A workforce platform goes further. Sully.ai integrates with MEDHOST and adds the AI Coder that submits clean claims, plus reception and triage, through one integration sized to community-hospital teams. What an AI Scribe Adds to the MEDHOST Workflow An AI scribe listens to the encounter and turns the conversation into a structured note. The clinician talks to the patient like normal. The scribe drafts the note in seconds, and the clinician reviews it instead of typing it. Community hospitals feel the charting load everywhere, and nowhere more than the ED, where MEDHOST's EDIS runs the highest-pressure documentation setting in the building. The numbers below are the burden a scribe is meant to remove. The difference on MEDHOST is that this is purely a third-party question. There is no native scribe to turn on, so the whole decision is which outside tool to add and how far past the note it goes. Ambient Documentation Versus Manual Charting The old flow is typing in MEDHOST during or after the encounter. Either way the clinician is still doing data entry, on the floor or in the ED. The ambient flow is listen, draft, review, sign. The impact is measurable: in a multi-site randomized study, ambient scribes cut documentation time meaningfully [4]. In a hospital, the question that decides real value is what happens to that note after it is written, because the note feeds coding, billing, and follow-up. MEDHOST Has No Native Scribe, So You Add One Many EHR vendors now ship a native ambient scribe. MEDHOST does not. Its product family covers the MEDHOST EHR, EDIS, revenue cycle, and patient engagement, with no native ambient documentation product [3]. So the decision here is not native versus third-party. It is which third-party tool, and how deeply it connects. Almost nobody answers that plainly for MEDHOST, which is why this guide starts there. How AI Scribes Connect to MEDHOST Because there is no native option, the choices are a lightweight cross-EHR scribe, an enterprise ambient platform, or a workforce platform. The depth decides how much of the administrative load a tool actually removes. The key distinction for a community hospital: documenting the encounter and automating the work around it are not the same thing, and neither is a light overlay the same as an enterprise rollout. Integration type Documents the visit Beyond the note Deployment weight Connection Lightweight cross-EHR scribe Yes None Light, fast Overlay or paste Enterprise ambient platform Yes Limited Enterprise contract Embed or integration Workforce platform Yes Claims, reception, triage One integration Deep integration Lightweight Cross-EHR Scribes The fastest route. Tools like Freed run as an extension or overlay and push a chart-ready note into the EHR [6]. These are good for lean teams that want speed and low cost. The tradeoff is that the connection is shallow and the tool stops at the note. It does not code-to-claim or staff the front desk. Enterprise Ambient Platforms Nuance DAX Copilot and Abridge document at scale and are deepest in Epic, and Suki markets a cross-EHR ambient assistant to community hospitals [5][7][8]. They document well. The tradeoff for a community hospital is weight and scope. These are documentation tools, typically contract-priced and deployed as enterprise projects, and they do not submit clean claims or staff the front desk. Workforce Platforms The broadest tier. A workforce platform integrates with MEDHOST and adds agents across the encounter. Sully.ai integrates with MEDHOST once, and then its agents share that connection: the AI Scribe documents, the AI Coder submits the claim, the AI Receptionist handles scheduling, and the AI Triage Nurse runs intake. This is the option that goes past the note, through one integration rather than an enterprise rollout. How to Add an AI Scribe to MEDHOST Step by Step Five steps take you from decision to a validated note in the chart. 1. Confirm Your MEDHOST Footprint and Goals Confirm what you run, the MEDHOST EHR on the floors and EDIS in the ED, and identify the clinical-informatics owner. Since there is no native scribe, decide what you want from a third-party tool: just a note, where a lightweight scribe is the quick win, or coding into claims, scheduling, and triage, which points to a workforce platform. That goal determines the route. 2. Choose Your Integration Method Map the methods to that goal. A lightweight scribe is fastest and documents only. An enterprise ambient platform documents at scale and deploys as an enterprise project. A workforce platform handles claims, reception, and triage through one integration. The decision rule: a lightweight tool is the fast way to get a note, but it stops at the note. If you want the work after the encounter handled, the claim submitted plus scheduling and triage, without an enterprise project, you need a workforce platform. 3. Connect the Scribe For a lightweight tool, sign in alongside MEDHOST. For an enterprise or workforce tool, have the vendor integrate with your MEDHOST environment [5][6]. Whichever route you pick, two things are non-negotiable before any patient audio is recorded: a signed BAA and HIPAA-compliant data handling, reviewed against your hospital's data-governance policy. 4. Map Notes and Coding to MEDHOST Configure how each note section maps to the correct MEDHOST fields, including ED notes in EDIS, and how codes attach to each problem instead of landing as one block. A lightweight scribe leaves placement shallow; a workforce platform writes coded, claim-ready data . Verify it against the templates and service lines you actually run, not a demo. 5. Pilot in the ED, Measure, and Scale Pilot where the pressure is highest, and in most community hospitals that is the ED. The busiest shift is the one that reveals real value. Confirm the note lands in the right MEDHOST sections, measure the time saved , which is well documented for ambient scribes [4], and measure the work after the note: are claims cleaner, is follow-up handled. Validate governance before a hospital-wide rollout. What to Look For in a MEDHOST AI Scribe Four criteria separate the tools on the shortlist. Community-Hospital Fit Enterprise ambient platforms price and deploy for large systems. A community hospital needs a tool that goes live with a lean IT team and a budget that makes sense at community scale. Match the deployment weight to your team, and weigh the cost against what the tool actually replaces, not just the seat price. Depth of Work After the Note Does the tool turn the encounter into linked ICD-10 and CPT codes and a clean claim, and handle scheduling and follow-up, or just document? Lightweight and enterprise scribes document. Workforce platforms go further. This is where the real value sits for a hospital running its own billing operation. Sully pairs its AI Scribe with an AI Coder that extracts every ICD-10 and CPT code and submits clean claims, plus front-desk and triage agents. Coverage From the ED to the Floor A hospital scribe has to work where the pressure is: the ED on EDIS, the inpatient units, and any owned clinics. Ask each vendor where the tool actually works in your MEDHOST environment, and confirm it against your service lines rather than a demo. Security, Governance, and HIPAA Compliance The non-negotiables: HIPAA compliance, a signed BAA, encryption and de-identified PHI handling , MFA, SSO, role-based access, and clear retention controls. Keep the review practical. Ask where audio is processed, how long recordings are retained, who can access transcripts, and whether the vendor will sign your BAA before the pilot starts. Best AI Scribes for MEDHOST Five tools worth shortlisting. MEDHOST has no native scribe to list, so these are all third-party. 1. Sully.ai Sully.ai starts as a strong ambient scribe on MEDHOST and extends into a coordinated AI workforce through a single integration. The AI Scribe documents the encounter, then the AI Coder extracts ICD-10 and CPT codes and submits clean claims, the AI Receptionist handles calls and scheduling, and the AI Triage Nurse runs intake and follow-up. Three things set it apart on MEDHOST. First, it goes past the note: the other scribes on this list document, while Sully also codes the claim and staffs the front desk and triage. Second, it is one integration and a connected workforce sized to community-hospital teams, not an enterprise rollout. Third, breadth and proven scale: Sully integrates with MEDHOST and also with Epic, Cerner, Meditech, Athenahealth, and more than 20 other EHRs, across 5,000+ providers and 50M+ hours of AI work delivered. Each AI role costs 80 to 90% less than the equivalent human role. Best fit: community hospitals on MEDHOST that want documentation plus the administrative work after the note handled by one connected team. 2. Suki A cross-EHR ambient AI assistant marketed to community hospitals and health systems, with ambient documentation and dictation [5]. Standout: community-hospital positioning and voice features. Best fit: hospitals that want an ambient documentation assistant, after confirming MEDHOST fit. 3. Nuance DAX Copilot Microsoft and Nuance's enterprise ambient documentation, embedded in major EHRs and typically contract-priced per provider [7]. Standout: established enterprise documentation with deep Microsoft backing. Best fit: systems standardized on Microsoft tooling, after confirming MEDHOST fit and community-scale pricing. 4.
